extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded investigators, PIs preparing JIT requests and RPPR/progress reports
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on responding to NIH Just-In-Time (JIT) requests and preparing Research Performance Progress Reports (RPPRs)/progress reports for Program Officers and Grants Management so as to avoid award delays and present progress clearly. Covers timing, audience, content expectations, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress Report audience and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your NIH grant Progress Report goes to Program. Your PO. It does not go to any SRO or study section members... It is for the consumption of the IC that funded your grant. It forms the non-competing application for your next interval of support that has already passed competitive review muster.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the RPPR for the Program Officer/IC that funds the grant — it is the non-competing continuation application, not a document for peer reviewers or study sections. Tailor content to the IC/PO perspective and the award interval rather than to reviewers' critique style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write RPPRs seriously but concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: "Just write them as if you take it seriously and everyone will probably be happy with it. It is not a ready-to-submit-manuscript level of report.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, well-organized summaries of progress and outputs; you need not produce a full manuscript, but avoid slapdash one-liners. Clarity and concise communication are valued; include enough detail to show meaningful progress without overburdening the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the PO's life easier / show effort and enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you ever need a PO to make a case for you when you're on the margin, doing things to make their lives easier is a good thing... I get super-excited when reading ones where the PI's effort and enthusiasm about their progress comes through (common among newer investigators).",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure reports so POs can quickly grasp progress, issues, and needs. Highlight PI effort, key accomplishments, interesting problems or negative results. Clear presentation increases the chance a PO will advocate for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling last year's report with minimal edits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Fastest way to get a request for additional information? Send me last year's report with two sentences changed.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit essentially the same RPPR repeatedly. Even small, superficial changes trigger additional information requests from PO/GMS; instead provide substantive updates on activities, milestones, and outcomes since the last report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect variability in PO engagement but assume they read RPPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments and author: POs sometimes read them closely and sometimes only skim; but many POs do read and track portfolio; it's part of their job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume your PO will at least skim your RPPR. Because POs vary, err on the side of clarity and completeness; a well-written RPPR can help when decisions are marginal.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIT (Just-In-Time) requests are automated and relatively generous
rubrics_metrics.description: "the eRA commons automailbot sends out requests for your JIT (Other Support page, IRB/IACUC approvals) information within weeks of your grant receiving a score... The point is, that it is incredibly generous... when you look at your score and think 'that is a no-way-it-will-ever-fund score' and still get the JIT autobot request, this doesn't mean you are wrong. It means the autobot was set to email you at a very generous threshold.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret an automated JIT email as a firm sign of imminent funding — thresholds can be generous and vary by IC/mechanism. Treat the request seriously and supply requested materials promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical JIT score threshold (practical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commenters: JIT/automated notices commonly go to applications receiving an impact score of 40 or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally, expect automated JIT notices for applications scoring roughly ≤40 under current/previous impact scoring rules, but confirm with specific IC guidance since cutoffs may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to JIT requests and GMS requests promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: "JIT information is also requested by the Grants Management Specialist when he/she is working on preparing your award, post-Council. DEFINITELY respond to this request.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely responses to JIT and GMS requests (Other Support, IRB/IACUC approvals) are crucial to avoid award delays. If JIT comes early (autobot), you may have time to finalize approvals; by the time GMS requests it, missing approvals will likely delay award start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use JIT timing to finalize IRB/IACUC approvals but update when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only advantage I see to the autobot request is that if you need to finalize anything with your IRB or IACUC this gives you time. By the time the GMS requests it, you are probably going to be delaying your award if you do not have IRB/IACUC approval in hand. If you submit your Other Support page with the autobot request, you are just going to have to update it anyway after Council.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If JIT arrives early, use that window to obtain human-subjects/animal approvals. Beware submitting Other Support or approvals too early — be prepared to submit updated materials after Council or before award if circumstances change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and be prepared for PRAM/additional materials requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment mention: receiving PRAM (progress report additional materials) requests occurs — POs sometimes ask for extra materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep underlying data, figures, and documentation ready in case the PO requests additional materials; prepare supplemental materials succinctly and linked to claims in the RPPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIs' outputs (publications) strongly influence PO perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment observation: "What they really care about are publications, and i suspect don't really give a flying fucke about any PI babbling in the progress report.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize concrete outputs such as publications, submitted manuscripts, patents, and measurable milestones. While clear narrative is valuable, documented outputs carry significant weight in PO assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in RPPR length and content depending on PO expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotal practices range from detailed reports with figures to short paragraph updates without figures; POs' preferences vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt level of detail to the project and PO expectations: new investigators may benefit from more context and enthusiasm; established PIs sometimes use shorter updates. When in doubt, be concise but include key accomplishments and outputs.
